utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Hopefully they will be making space in this court. Mr. Registrar, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, assisted by my case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to my learned friends of the Prosecution, to everyone in and around the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson on behalf of General Delic, with our legal assistant, Lana Deljkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see the witness has just walked into court. May the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. For the record, can you please state your full name, spelling your last name, please.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Sead Delic. S-e-a-d D-e-l-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, can you please state your place of birth and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 13th of September, 1954 in the town of Gorazde, Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, are you related to the accused, Rasim Delic, in this case?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: No, not in any way. I am not related to General Rasim Delic. We were born in different parts of -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was born in the north, and I was born in the south-east of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, can you please briefly tell the Trial Chamber about your career from the time you left school until the present time.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: In several sentences, I would tell you that my career consisted of the following: In 1977 I completed the military academy for land forces in Belgrade after four years of attendance. Then I was promoted to the lowest officer rank, this being second lieutenant. After that, I served in Tuzla, where I was appointed commander of the reconnaissance platoon or company. I stayed there for three years. After that, in the same town, in the same corps and the same division, for six years I was company commander at the corps for detachment leaders. After that, I was for two years battalion commander in the same town in the same unit. In 1989 I was sent to school again at the Command Staff Academy for Ground Forces in Belgrade, where I spent two years, between 1989 and 1991, until June of that year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The various positions held by the witness in Tuzla were in which army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This all pertains to the pre-war period, when I was an active duty officer with the JNA in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. We can proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you left off at the point where you were telling us about attendance at the Command Staff Academy for Ground Forces in Belgrade, from 1989 until 19 -- until June 1991. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what you did after June 1991.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Upon completing the Command Staff Academy, I was assigned to a new duty in Croatia in Varadzin, to the corps. At that corps I was with them until the 15th or 16th of September, 1992; that is, from July until September 1991. And I took part in the initial combat activities in the territory of the Republic of Croatia. In 1991, in the corps command, where I was assigned assistant staff commander for operational and educational affairs, I was wounded and I was transferred to the military medical academy in Belgrade. I was treated there for about 32 or 33 days, after which I returned to Tuzla. As after the 1st of December until the 10th of April, the 1st of December, 1991, until the 10th of April, I stayed there. And at that -- on that date, I officially left the JNA. During that period, I worked half time four hours a day, and the rest was spent at various treatments that I had to undergo because of the wounding. I left the JNA on the 10th of April, 1992 officially, having turned over all of the documentation during the four previous days. I simply decided that that armed force was no longer the same armed force that I pledged to serve because of all the things it did to various people in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. I decided I no longer wanted to stay with that army. I handed over the rules, all of the documentation, as well as equipment that I was issued with, and I left the Yugoslav People's Army. On the 14th of April, 1992, I joined the then-Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or rather, to the Territorial Defence of Tuzla municipality, although even before that day I had contacts with that organisation. Between the 14th and the 19th; however, there is an order dated the 22nd of April as well -- in that period, I was elected by the Crisis Staff of the Municipality of Tuzla to act as military advisor with an additional two officers. On the 19th of April, on the recommendation, or rather, appointment, since there was no other possibility at the time, I was appointed to a new duty by the head of municipality, Mr. Beslagic. I was appointed commander of the Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence of Tuzla, which was newly formed after the former TO had been disbanded and the new one formed. Between that date and until the end of the war, I had the following duties: Commander of the TO Tuzla Municipal Staff, which later was renamed to become the 5th operational group of the 2nd Corps of the Army of BH. And in October 1994, I was appointed commander of the 2nd Corps. I stayed there until the end of the war, according to the wartime establishment. Once the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina was over, I remained at the position of commander of the 2nd Corps of the Army of the Federation until the 1st of October, 2000. As of that date, on my request, I was retired, after which I had several different duties and jobs, such as lecturer at the University of Tuzla. Apart from that, in 2002. I was elected to the Federation parliament, where I spent four years. I was deputy at the Federal Parliament. I am currently retired, without any particular titles or obligations to attend to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, at the time you retired from the Army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina on 1 October 2000, what rank did you hold?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: When I was retired, I was major general of the Army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you tell us, at that point in time, in October 1994, when you were appointed the commander of the 2nd Corps, can you briefly tell us, sir, what the duties and responsibilities of a corps commander in the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina consisted of?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is very difficult to put it in a few sentences only. I need to tell you, though - and you probably heard this from other people - that during that period there was reorganisation. Before that, the Territorial Defence had been disbanded as it existed and per tasks it used to have in the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. A new Territorial Defence was formed headed by Hasan Efendic, the then-Minister for Territorial Defence. I believe the minister was Jerko Doko. Before the formation of the corps, what there was in existence was the County Staff of the Territorial Defence. Its function was to try and unify the activity of all units in the territory of the North-Eastern Bosnia, the 13 municipality in that part of Bosnia. If need be, I can enumerate them, starting with Tuzla being the centre, then Kladanj, Teocak and the rest. In any case, 13 municipalities. That county staff, or regional staff, later became the 2nd Corps. As far as I can remember, an order on formation of the 2nd Corps of the then-Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina took place on the 29th of September, 1992. The force was simply renamed. I don't think anything else of significance took place. The same personnel, the same commands, with its establishment changed to a lesser degree. It was simply assigned a new name and a new role. In brief, I wanted to say that the role of the corps at that time, during wartime activities, boiled down to basically attempting to unify all of the forces in the area of the North-Eastern Bosnia and to coordinate resistance and defence against aggression. At that period, one city and town were lost after another: Zvornik, Bijeljina, Kalesija fell without fight, and they managed to reach 10 kilometres away from Tuzla. By the time the division was already in place, the rift and the JNA had already armed all of the Serb population and took up all key positions in various municipalities. At that time, the main goal of the corps was to have all those 13 towns or municipalities to try and assist each other in reaching their common goal. Before that time, such attempts were not in place. For example, the people of Tuzla did not even try to defend Bijeljina, because they were concerned for their own lives in Tuzla. In Tuzla, there were several thousand soldiers and officers of the former JNA. The story is long, but in essence the function of the corps boiled down to trying to organise the whole area to defend itself. The corps had nothing at its disposal. It had no logistics and the people who were in the command of the corps even did not have their own meals. I provided food for them from the Municipal Staff. Each municipality had its own Crisis Staff and it managed it. As far as the rest goes, the people at the top were there merely trying to do whatever was possible at any given moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, I appreciate the depth of knowledge that you bring to these issues, but, sir, for the sake of time I'm going to ask you to please focus on the questions - excuse me - that I ask and try to answer those, and you'll be given ample opportunity to explain those answers if the need arises. But let me ask you this, sir: At the time you assumed command of the 2nd Corps of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in October 1994, how many men were in the 2nd Corps? How many men did you have in your corps?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: The situation -- the situation changed with time. It was not the same thing to be in 1992 or in 1994. When I was appointed, I already had around 86,000 people. Through additional reorganisation, parts of operational groups would be made part of the corps, and then they would leave. In any case, the manning strength was around 80,000, the highest figure being 86,000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, General, where were the men in the 2nd Corps from? Where did those men come from?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Members of the 2nd Corps came from the 13 municipality of what now is the Tuzla canton, as well as the refugees from other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I would ask you now to focus your attention on the western sector of the 2nd Corps area of responsibility, and can you tell the Trial Chamber, please, the situation in the summer of 1995 on the western sector of your, that is, the 2nd Corps area of responsibility ever. What was the situation like there?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the summer of 1995, I would say, was the time when the situation was most difficult in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps. In June there was a genocide committed over the Bosniaks in the protected and demilitarised zone in Srebrenica and Zepa. The focus of activity of the 2nd Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was then directed at that part of the front, trying to rescue civilians and some military recruits which used the corridor to pass through the safe territory. The forces merely tried to save those people. As for the rest of the front, as stated by the Prosecutor, there were combat operations in place of a lesser extent, trying to disable the enemy to engage their full potential in the area of Srebrenica and Zepa. If specifically you are asking me about the Vozuca pocket, I can tell you that it represented a grave problem before the 2nd Corps and the 3rd Corps, since these were adjacent corps. The Vozuca pocket included Mount Ozren, and valley of the Krivaja River and northwards to the Spreca, the front line was around 100 kilometres and some four brigades were permanently engaged there. Two, I believe, were within the 3rd Corps and two within my corps, that is, the 2nd Corps. That very pocket prevented us from establishing communication between the regions of Zenica and Tuzla. The pocket was of high strategic importance for us in order to be able to transfer some forces elsewhere and to try and establish better communication with Zenica. Until that time, we had to go via Vares and other areas in order to reach Zenica. It was very difficult, since the terrain there is inaccessible and one could only move about in off-road vehicles and in some trucks. Some tunnels had to be worked on in order to make them bigger so that the trucks could go through. Mount Zvjijezda is a very difficult mountain to cross, and all that made the Vozuca pocket our priority. Before I was appointed commander, several corps commanders tried to deal with that problem unsuccessfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask now, with the assistance of the Registry and the usher, if the witness could be shown the electronic version of Exhibit 380. And I would ask that he be assisted with using the electronic pen to make some markings on that map, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have the electronic pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could please put the map into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You were asked that were assisted --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could have the map into the middle part of the map, please. No, don't zoom in, please. I want to see -- that's -- if we could just go down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, can you see that map before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see the map. But, please, could we see it a little better, please? Closer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me -- let me explain what I'm going to ask you to do, sir, and I think that we perhaps could then zoom in to a particular part of the map. I'm going to ask you if it's possible for you -- you've mentioned Ozren. I'm wondering if you could on this map draw the possible locations of what was known as the Ozren front in 1995. And if we need to zoom in a little bit, we can, but -- we need to do that before. So if you can on this map mark the entire Ozren front line.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I might be mistaken by a margin of 500 or 1,000 metres, because I'm not really familiar closely with the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, but I'll try. The front line went down the valley of Krivaja River, then from the confluence of Krivaja River into Bosna River, and it was approximately there, the valley of Bosna River from one side or the other in the direction of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry, General, but you can actually place that pen - it's an electronic pen - on the screen and actually draw. If you could actually draw on the screen the front line and -- and the places that you've just indicated. So if you could actually just draw right on the screen with the electronic pen, please.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand. The problem here is I can't see the map very well. It's too small.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me. Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder, before prosecuting counsel goes any further with trying to get the witness to draw the front line, bearing in mind what he said, that he was not familiar with the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, could the Prosecutor establish whether he was actually aware of where the front line was before he attempts -- he's asked to actually attempt to draw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would draw your attention to line 10 of page 11, where he said I might be mistaken by a margin of 500 or 1000 metres. That certainly would imply, but I can ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, were you familiar with the general area of the front line with respect to the 3rd Corps on the Ozren front?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Not the 3rd Corps but my own corps, yes; although, I was once also on part of the line of responsibility in the Vozuca theatre of war and in the 3rd Corps. Based on the documents I had access to, I can draw this line roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask that the witness be allowed to do that. And, again, we're simply -- we're simply offering this for the general location of what the Ozren front was or area what the Ozren front was that will assist with the witness's testimony so that we all know when he talks about the Ozren front what he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you asking the witness to draw the front line of the 3rd Corps, or are you asking him to draw the Ozren front line, or are you asking him to draw the front line of the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps -- perhaps before I do that, let me -- allow me to ask a couple of additional questions to the witness, and I think it might be a little bit more clearer in terms of what exactly it is I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, can you tell us which armed forces were aligned on the Ozren front?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: On the Ozren front, from the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps of the BH army, there was the 223rd and 225th Brigades of the 2nd Corps of the BH army; that is, a brigade formed from the population of Banovici municipality and one brigade formed from the population of Lukavac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What other armed forces were on or about the Ozren front?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: I was talking about this part of the Vozuca operation, because I thought that was of interest to you. But please bear in mind there was another brigade from Gracanica municipality and Doboj east, which covered the north and north-east in the direction of Doboj, down the valley of Spreca River, defending the population of this municipality. So Banovici, Lukavac, Gracanica, and Doboj East brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, other than ARBiH 2nd Corps units, what military force or forces were deployed along the Ozren front?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: From what I know, those were units of the 3rd Corps of the BH army, which were then grouped in the 35th Division of the 3rd Corps. I'm not only sure about the Olovo Brigade, but I believe that one too was in the south-east part. Whether it formed part of the 31st Division or it was part of the 1st Corps, I'm not sure, but it was located in this area and engaged there for a while during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than the ARBiH units, sir, were there any other military forces on the Ozren front?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Apart from the BH army, in that time of offensive operations, I only heard about the El Mujahid Detachment, but no other units. I don't think HVO units were part of these operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps my question's not clear, sir, but the ARBiH units that you've told us about from 2nd and 3rd Corps, were they opposed to any other military forces on the Ozren front?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: From what I know, no. There were Serbian forces that were defending if that's what you meant, the Serb, Chetnik enemy forces, yes. Certainly. I hadn't understood you at first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I gathered as much initially, sir. Yeah, that's exactly what I'm talking about, these Serb Chetnik enemy forces as you've described them. Were you generally familiar with the Ozren front in the period of the summer of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was familiar with that front.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately -- approximately how long was the front line at Ozren, or the Ozren front line? How long was that front line?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't measure it, but I reckon it is around 100 kilometres from beginning to end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What, sir, were the primary geographic features which delineated the Ozren front line?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: The main features, in my view, were these: That the former JNA, before combat operations began, armed the entire population and brought other people from the area of Doboj and Doboj itself, and they captured the main elevations that controlled the valley of Bosna River and Spreca River. Their main reliance militarily was on Mount Ozren, because it had a dominant position between these two rivers and practically divided two regions, two geographic regions: The region of Tuzla and the Zenica region. And that was a lifeline in the economic sense and every other sense, including, of course, militarily. You have to bear in mind that Doboj is a communication hub of inestimable value for Tuzla, for instance, because I personally think that Tuzla is communication-wise a dead-end, because it does not have much importance in this area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, despite its economic and the demographic potential. So to conclude, Ozren and the Ozren front line was extremely important. Vozuca is a small village on the way from Banovici to Zavidovici villages in which half the population were Serbs, half were Bosniaks. Bosniaks were immediately expelled as soon as the war started. And for Serbs, it remained some sort of base. That's why you find frequent references to Vozuca as the Vozuca pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, in light of the comments that you've just given us, are you in a position, sir, to draw the rough front lines that constituted the Ozren front in the summer of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: If I say "yes," I don't think I'll be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask you, sir, with that electronic pen to draw the Ozren front line to the best of your recollection as it was in summer 1995.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: [Marks] That would be roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, can you place, sir, what you've described as the Serb or Chetnik forces, can you please write on the map where the Serb or Chetnik forces were located in the summer of 1995.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Right here, where I drew these lines. So that is approximately 200, 300 metres to the east, north, and south. Those are the positions of the BH army. And inside this pocket were enemy forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. That -- that's my question, sir: When you say "inside," can you please write the initials of the armed force that was inside. Just write it right on the map, what -- the initials of the armed force that was "inside," as you've put it.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly the names of those brigades, but I know there was a brigade from Pribava. It's this area here --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry, General, sorry to interrupt. I'm not particularly interested in the brigades. I'm simply interested in which armed force was on the "inside," as you've put it?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska was here, or the JNA. They were both. They were in this area outside the pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what military force was outside of the line that you've drawn?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Outside the line I drew, to the east, the 2nd Corps. Approximately up to here in the south. And all the way to Doboj -- or rather, the suburbs of Doboj town and the Bosna River. Now, to the west and south-west and north-west were the forces of the 3rd Corps of the BH army. I think at that time the 35th Division was there and it held this area with part of its forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask that this map be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The map is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 397.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask that the witness be shown the document previously marked P002277. That's P002277.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we getting the document P002277 now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- I do have a number of documents to show this witness. And if we're experiencing delays, I do have hard copies, if that would assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's have hard copies, because it looks like we're having a bit of a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, do you see the document on the screen in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: There are two documents here. I don't know which one you mean. This must be the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask you, sir, to look at the Bosnian version of the document.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this document is, please.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: This document requests that reports be submitted by the commands of the 2nd and 3rd Corps; namely, an interim report on progress during operations on the Ozren front. Somebody signed -- in fact, it says "Rasim Delic, the army general, should have been there, but somebody signed on his behalf, maybe an authorised person. We see initials "TF."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, General Delic, unfortunately there's a -- there's a slight omission in the English translation of this document. Can you tell us to whom this document was addressed?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: It's addressed to the command of the 2nd and the 3rd Corps of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 398.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, can you briefly tell the Trial Chamber what activities or what the results achieved in the activities on the Ozren front were at this point in time; that is, on or about 21 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Without a map and without reminding myself of those precise dates, I couldn't really say. But as far as I recall, Your Honours, in this period, in those ten days - that's ten days from the beginning of the operation - the planned part of the operation had been completed and further actions continued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Counsel for the Defence is on his feet. Let's hear what he has got to say before you carry on. Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Before the witness continued, I was just I was going to ask if prosecuting counsel could establish whether or not this witness was actually aware of what was going on on or about the 21st of July. It seems that there's a -- it was rather led to him that he had information or knowledge about events at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't understand what you're asking, Mr. Robson. Was this witness not part of the operations in the Ozren pocket, in the Vozuca pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe it's been established that he was involved in activities in the Vozuca pocket in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In July 1995. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document doesn't talk about the Vozuca pocket specifically. It talks about the Ozren front. The witness has testified about that, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I thought. And I thought July 1995 is the date of the document. It's just it's not giving a time of the activities -- time of the report to be given. It just says "give us a report on the activities on the Ozren front." Mr. Robson, I still don't understand you are -- what you are asking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just suggesting that it was -- it was a leading question, because it hadn't been established that General Delic here was actually involved in combat activities, operations, on the Ozren front in July 1995. If it has been, I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. Rather object than give advice, because then when you give advice, I -- first of all, I wonder why you are giving advice to your opposite member. But if you object, then it makes better sense to me. I understand what you are saying. But also on this specific objection - if it is an objection - I am saying the 21st of July is the date of this document. Presumably, given the content of the document, it is asking of results of activities that took place prior to the date of this document. It's asking for a report. So it's not necessarily asking this witness to tell us about activities in July. It's asking this witness to tell us about activities on the Ozren front, whenever they took place. They might have taken place in December or on 13th month, which is whose name I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes. You may proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question, Mr. Delic: I asked you to tell the Trial Chamber what activities or what the results achieved in the activities on the Ozren front were at this point in time, that is, on or about 21 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I caused confusion because I hadn't understood the date properly. In that period, speaking of the 2nd Corps, the focus was on the east part of the front; namely, trying to save the people from Zepa and Srebrenica. Now, as far as the Ozren front is concerned, we can say that there were only negligible activities. If I remember correctly, those were activities of the 225th Brigade, or to be more precise, the Lukavac Brigade, which had then succeeded through local operations, small-scale operations, to capture two elevations in the area of responsibility it was defending. So practically in that period, we did whatever we could not only in this part of the front, but in our entire area of responsibility, to tie up the enemy and to relieve as far as we could the suffering of the people from Zepa and Srebrenica. I'm sorry, I had previously misunderstood the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, can you explain to the Trial Chamber in the period of July and August 1995 what taskings or objectives the 2nd Corps was asked by the Main Staff to complete?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we were all focused then on saving people and saving whatever we could from Podrinje, Zepa, and Srebrenica. We tried to form a unit of sorts from the able-bodied men who were there, but that unit never took part in actual fighting until the end of the war. We tried to gather intelligence and to find out what kind of crime was committed in Zepa and Srebrenica. In that period, before the actual events in Zepa and Srebrenica, there were activities to lift the blockade of Sarajevo, as you probably know. A smaller part of the units, one or two brigades strong from the 2nd Corps were involved in that. After all the following events, after NATO airstrikes and failed negotiations, we tried to implement the part of the directive that was received by the command of the 2nd Corps early that year or at the end of the previous year. That corps, which was completely independent, had to select assignments that were only roughly outlined and try to carry them out. One of them was to free the Vozuca pocket. There had been several unsuccessful attempts previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, let me -- let me interrupt you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness be shown the document that's been marked PT003064. And if I neglected to do so, I would tender the document dated 21 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document, 21 July, was it not Exhibit 398?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, it was, Your Honour. I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask that the witness be shown PT003064.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, do you see the document on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It is a plan of coordination of the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina for the month of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could please go to page 12 of the Bosnian version and page 14 of the English version of this document. And specifically Roman numeral 13, paragraph 1 of Roman numeral 13. General Delic, do you see Roman numeral 13, subparagraph 1?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It contains the tasks of the 2nd Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, for the period of August 1995, what were those tasks as set forth in this document?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that these tasks were copied from my coordination plan. They state that the offensive combat activities plan should be put in -- in practice in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps with the focus of the zone of responsibility of the 22nd Division towards Vozuca, the 24th Division of ground forces towards Podrinje, and the 25th Division on Majevica, as well as preparing and sending of units of the 2nd Corps by the order of the General Staff of the ARBiH issued in accordance with special plan. The second task reads: "accommodation, restoring of work and life" -- I believe it says "work and life or functioning."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: As well as carrying -- I cannot see the end. We should move on to page 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's okay, General. I was primarily interested in the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry the document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 399.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We would ask that the witness be shown the document marked PT003065, PT003065.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, do you see the document on the screen in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is a document of the administration of military security, which was part of the General Staff. Pertaining to the plan of coordination of the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina for the month of September of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask, please, that we go to page 15 in the English version and the page stamped -- in the Bosnian version, the page stamped with ERN number 06084931. 06084931. The bottom part of the Bosnian version, please. General, I draw your attention to paragraph Roman numeral 12, subparagraph 1. Can you take a look at that, please.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. I mentioned that previously. I have to say, Your Honours, that the coordination plan is meant to regulate in general the life and work in various units. I believe this is an excerpt from my plan of organising life and work and activities for this month. It says: "Conducting the plan for offensive combat operations in the 2nd Corps area of responsibility, according to the special plan, focusing on the -- on the Uragan plan." And: "Performing obligations following conclusions and tasks of the General Staff of the Army of the BH." Strictly confidential. I cannot see the number. I think it says "01/015-1."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We're interested, again, mainly in the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would tender this document into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number. Yes, Judge, just before you do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, I have a question to you relating these last pieces of evidence that you have introduced. And I don't know if it would be appropriate to ask the witness to take off his earphones, provided he does not speak and understand English. Do you know if he does?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It's my understanding that he understands very limited English, but perhaps I can ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Then please ask him to remove his earphones just for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, just please take off the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I -- I simply have a difficulty in understanding what it is you wish the Chamber to elicit from these pieces of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What are they supposed to show?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: These documents show that the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was tasking the corps commanders with undertaking certain operations relating to Vozuca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But that couldn't come as a surprise, could it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, again, Your Honours, I have a firm obligation to prove my case and in the absence of agreements from the Defence as to the role of the accused Rasim Delic in the combat operations going on under which the crimes in this indictment were committed, I have an obligation, I believe, to put all of this evidence before the Trial Chamber. I'd be in a different situation if there were some additional agreed facts coming from the Defence, but at this point in time, we -- we don't have any agreed facts concerning these operations, and I have a duty to show that the Main Staff was directing from the beginning the coordination and planning of these military operations and these documents, in my respectful submission, go to that very point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And may I ask the Defence if they have any objections against the authenticity of these plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't object to the authenticity of these documents, but in our submission, this goes back to the issue that I raised yesterday evening, because rather like the evidence we -- that the Trial Chamber heard yesterday, again, documents are being put to a witness without then following on and putting to the witness the importance or relevance of those documents. We today have prepared cross-examination on the basis of many, many documents. And now because the -- the Prosecutor has raised these documents, has not asked further questions, essentially an inference could arise from those documents. The Trial Chamber could -- could look at those documents in the future and draw an inference from it. It means that in addition to all the other points that I was going to raise anyway, I now have to deal with each and every one of these documents myself in cross-examination and try and, if you like, undo any inference that may be drawn. So, again, Your Honours, the Defence's submission is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But maybe we should invite the parties to then increase their level of cooperation, because -- I mean, I -- I don't know if the -- if you, as Defence team, would have any objections against accepting that these combat operations were carried out and planned in accordance with the normal structures that were applicable in the BiH; that is to say, that they somehow, I guess, were coordinated or planned in coordination with the -- with the -- with the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Your Honour, I think the simple answer to that is that there would be difficulty in -- in reaching agreement on these documents, because I suspect the parties would ask the Trial Chamber to draw a different conclusion. The Defence's position, you will find out in due course during cross-examination, but we certainly couldn't accept the position as it stands by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Okay. Then let us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can Judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me. But you forget that I very often follow the translation in French, and you are putting the interpreters in a very difficult position. There is a delay, a considerable delay in minutes as to what you say in English. So please, because I would like to understand what is being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: My only hope in this exchange of views is that it would somehow be made clear to the Chamber what the disagreement is, because it is very difficult for the Chamber to understand the meaning of these many, many documents that come and they are on the screen for a couple of minutes and the witness is not being asked very much about it and then we move on to the next document and to the next document, and so on. And it is extremely difficult for us to make out what we, you know, should pick up from these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And as I indicated yesterday evening, the Prosecution team is conceptualising ideas on better ways or more efficient ways to get the documents into evidence, and one of those possibilities would be for - and I just throw this out at this point in time because it's -- it's arisen now again - one of the -- one of the options that we are considering is that at -- in the very, very near future, perhaps as early as next week, some type of motion, tendering several hundred documents from the bar table so that we don't have to spend our time dealing with each and every document, to get it into evidence through a witness but we can, rather, focus our attention on the contents of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But if I -- oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me. I agree that this could be an option, but -- but, again, the -- the Chamber is in a difficult position if we are just being in a position where we are receiving a number of documents without any idea as to their probative value. What is it that they're supposed to prove? And that normally requires either an explanation from the party who brings the document or some illumination through a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honours. And, again, what -- what we are trying to do is focus our attention on what are -- what might be designated or identified as core documents or core exhibits. There are several hundred such exhibits that are referred to in our pre-trial brief, which, in my respectful submission, puts them into some kind of context or some type of understanding for the Trial Chamber. I'm very reluctant to be put into a situation or position where we have to explain the relevance of each and every document in the presence of a witness at the time it's being tendered or offered into evidence. In an ideal world, we would have ample opportunity and time to take the witness through each and every part of each and every document that goes into evidence. Unfortunately, the limitations are such that that's not always possible. Some documents, such as the one which -- or the last two documents I've shown to the witness, there are only very brief parts of those documents that have some relevance or probative value to the ultimate issues that the Trial Chamber must decide. Obviously I'm going to be in a position, hopefully, time permitting, to ask the witness questions about the -- the material that's stated in the documents, and in that respect, perhaps this discussion might be a bit premature as to these documents with this witness, but I -- but I will say that I am cognisant of the problem. I'm aware of the problem. We are endeavouring, in the limited time we have available, to put the documents and to lead the viva voce evidence that Your Honours need. I'm not saying that this is unique to this case. I've been involved in a number of cases here, as have my colleagues from the Defence. All cases before the International Tribunal are facing the same types of problems. It perhaps is a bit more tricky or difficult in cases that tend to be circumstantial and document heavy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just ask the witness a point. Mr. Mundis, you say here page 30, lines 8 to 11 or somewhere there: "Obviously I'm going to be in a position, hopefully, time permitted, to ask the witness questions about the material that's stated in the documents." You know, I guess what -- what Judge Harhoff is phrasing is if you asked those questions that you are saying, you know, you're going to ask later at the time when the document is on the screen, it would be much more helpful to the Trial Chamber to follow why the document is being tendered into evidence, because you begin to deal with the content of the document and you'll begin to deal maybe -- hopefully you will be finding out from the witness why that document was generated, who generated it, for what purpose. Then we will be able to follow. But if it's just a document, and you just read a paragraph and you tender it in, we are indeed at a loss. And -- and the alternative that you are thinking of, of tendering 100 documents at a time is even worse than what we are now talking about, because now we are going to be inundated with documents the relevance of which we do not know, and we don't even know in those documents which paragraph to concentrate on. So this method is still better than tendering hundreds of documents. But we -- and the reason the document has to come through a witness is precisely for that reason, that the witness can explain to -- to us the -- the importance of the document in the discussion before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I -- I understand that, Your Honours. As I've indicated, what we've now seen on the screen before us, there's a reference which the witness indicated, Plan Uragan, that's exactly going to be the subject of the bulk of the remaining time available for the direct examination, which led me earlier to indicate that this discussion, with respect to these documents and this witness, is -- is premature. But -- but again, let me assure you, with respect to -- to tendering a large number of documents from the bar table, that it is not and is not my intention nor will I be in a situation where I'm dumping hundreds of documents on the Trial Chamber or seeking to do that without a full explanation of the relevance of each and every one of those documents. I would not simply stand up here and tender into evidence 800 documents with no explanation whatsoever. If -- if we go down that path, the Chamber will have detailed explanations as to the relevance of each and every one of those documents and that the one thing that's holding me back from directing my team to start such a process is the huge amount of work that's required, without any indications from the Trial Chamber, whether that would be acceptable or not. If I devote a huge amount of resources to doing that only to find that it's all for naught, then -- then we will have problems on the Prosecution side. So we're looking at a number of different ways of getting the important evidence before Your Honours in such a way, obviously, that -- that it makes sense that you understand the relevance and the probative value of it. That's called good advocacy and that's one thing that I believe very strongly in -- in getting my team to do. And so I guarantee you I'm not going to stand up here and throw 800 documents at the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we break, can I ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we break, Madam Vidovic, you wanted to say something very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, briefly. Since now I learn of the existence of this option of tendering a large number of documents, I can tell you that it is certain that we would object to that. I believe it would be deeply unfair. However, if the Prosecutor indeed attempts to do such a thing, we will provide our explanation as to the objection that we have. As regards the way of tendering documents in this way, I can perhaps respond to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, I understand your sentiment. Let's not try to deal with the motion that's not before us. Let's deal with it when it comes. But I -- the sentiment -- the sentiment is understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I merely wanted to comment these two exhibits that were admitted last. I wanted to express our position. The Prosecutor drafted their indictment and their pre-trial brief in which they state that the accused took part in the planning of the July, September, and October combat activities in 1995. This Defence opposed this strongly in our pre-trial brief, and we put forth our position. These documents are very relevant, and the two witnesses you could see, for example, yesterday, who was deputy commander of the 3rd Corps and today commander of the 2nd Corps, are the people who are in good position to provide concrete answers as to what was actually going on. And they can also describe the importance of this document. Perhaps we can have a look at the witness's answer regarding this. It leaves me with the same doubt, the same question as His Honour Judge Harhoff. We do have to know what the Prosecutor intends to do with this document, where are they going with this? We need this to be able to prepare for cross-examination. We do not oppose this, but it is unfair to quote a small portion of the document, because this witness, more than any, can tell us more about the importance of this entire documents -- document. This is the gist of what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. Mr. Mundis has assured us that that complaint is a little premature. He's coming to it. Shall we take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we proceed, may we give that document an exhibit number, please. That is document PT003065.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be Exhibit number 400.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, General Delic, before the break we were talking about the document that we were looking at, and you said "I believe" -- and this is -- I'm quoting from lines 22 through 24 of page 24: "I believe this is an excerpt from my plan." And I'm wondering if you can tell us, sir, what you were referring to when you said "my plan."

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, my plans were never approved by the General Staff. Concerning my activities, I sent such plans to the General Staff with the general descriptions of tasks of my units and my command for the forthcoming month. Such documents were usually drafted at the beginning of every month, describing in general what the activities are to be undertaken, by whom, and at what time. I also had a column for remarks with any remarks that may be needed to explain. I believe this is an excerpt from one of such plans of mine; however, I believe that can be checked in the archives that you must have, although I'm quite sure that I am correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, General Delic, this exhibit, Exhibit number 400 that we were just looking at, indicates that there should be a focus on the Uragan plan. Can you tell us, sir, if you know, what the Uragan plan was.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the hurricane plan was an operation undertaken by the 2nd Corps units of the Army of B and H in order to occupy the so-called Vozuca pocket, and they were trying to fulfil their focal tasks, which were derived from a directive we received early that year. All those directives were quite similar to each other, though. I saw two such copies during the four years I was there. They would usually describe tasks in general. For example, for the 2nd Corps, one of such directives said that we should hold on to the free territory and attempt to liberate within my area of responsibility the territory held by the enemy. I also remember then in all those directives there was a mention of the Ozren pocket as well, since it was of great importance for the 2nd Corps and its positions in that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you proceed, I did hear the interpretation saying "the hurricane plan."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes. Can I -- I don't want to be accused of testifying, but the word "Uragan" in English means "hurricane."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I would -- I would ask, if it's possible, for the interpreters to use the term "Uragan," because the documents refer to "Uragan." Otherwise, we're going to have confusion between the documents and the transcript. So -- I don't want to tell the interpreters how to do their job, but I might suggest - and perhaps if the Defence concurs - that we use the term "Uragan," because that's what the witnesses and the documents are going to talk about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We concur with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, General Delic, can you briefly tell us if any units other than the 2nd Corps units were involved in the Ozren pocket area in the summer of 1995, other ARBiH units other than 2nd Corps units.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: If you meant my area of responsibility, the answer would be yes. I personally requested that a smaller unit from the Black Swans Brigade, about 100 or 120 men strong, be resubordinated to me for the purpose of carrying out combat assignments purely for the benefit of morale, because it was negligible compared to some 5.000 attackers, but I needed to tell my fighting men that somebody had come outside -- from outside to help out. On a couple of occasions, we engaged around 600 members of the civilian police. They controlled the liberated territory and helped establish authorities in that territory, searched the terrain, and controlled roads in that area, because I did not have enough forces for that. The BH army did not have enough resources to do that. I must emphasise that in that period the so-called 28th Division left the 2nd Corps. To be more precise, those were parts of the units from Srebrenica and from the 2nd Corps that formed the 28th Division, and some units from Zivinice formed a reserve. It was one battalion that was briefly there and was used only for searching the terrain when our units pursued the enemy behind the lines. Later it was returned to their original unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, can you tell the Trial Chamber, if you know, what the 3rd Corps was planning at the same time as Operation Uragan.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: In parallel with the Operation Uragan, I don't know what they planned. I know they planned their own operation that was called Farz, if that's what you mean. They were on the opposite side and in coordinated action with us. We needed to solve the issue of this Vozuca pocket. Although, I have to emphasise we had our own areas of responsibility that we strictly observed, and in the course of combat operation there were no major movements of individuals or units from one area to another. If that's what you meant. I'm not sure I understood the question correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's precisely what I meant, sir. And we'll return to the issue of Operation Farz in just a moment. I would now ask, sir, that you be given the opportunity to look at P002430. That's P002430. Do you see the document on the screen in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this document is.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: This is my own personal plan of activities for the purpose of carrying out combat operations as part of the Uragan 95 operation. In this plan, I regulated where, how, and with what units and resources needs to be done. This concerns reconnoitering and developing combat documentation for the forthcoming combat operations, called Uragan 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, General Delic, a few moments ago, as reflected on page 35, lines 9 through 11, you told us that plans were sent to the General Staff with general descriptions of tasks of your units and command. Is this document that you're looking at one of those such plans?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: No way. This is my own plan. It was done on my own accord. That was something I did for myself as a commander, to facilitate my own work. By planning, you see, nobody was supposed to approve it. This plan was made available to my subordinate officers, to acquaint them with the assignment and how the assignment should be performed, in what area. This is about the implementation of the monthly plan. The monthly plan, for instance, stipulates that during that month, the Uragan operation should be executed. And this is my own plan how to carry out the monthly plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 401.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness now be shown P01918. P01918.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, do you see the document on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. This document is very familiar. It's my own order for offensive combat operations in the part of the Ozren theatre of war; that is, Uragan 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, General Delic, is it correct, sir, that this document does not have a date?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is no date on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you -- can you explain why this document does not have a date?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: That's how I was trained. For this kind of document, it's not necessary to put a date. I believe it's part of the standard operations procedures. Because this is an order that together with the decision is one of the most important documents, if not the most important document, in the course of the operation under which these activities are implemented, and therefore there is no date. But there is a date on the working map. There is an end date for the operation. And in this order, in addition to measures of logistical support, there is a precise date, end date, by which all activities stipulated by the order should be completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, can you again, sir, briefly tell the Trial Chamber - excuse me - what this order encompasses, what is the purpose of this order and what does it do? What were you trying to do by issuing this order?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: This order, like all military orders, contains basic information about the enemy, his intentions, his disposition and deployment, and all we knew about the enemy. It should contain the assignment of the corps as a whole. And below, the assignments given to the subordinated parts of the corps; specifically, there are three divisions here. I issued assignments to these divisions and to the corps' artillery group, who are in direct contact with me. And we can see in this order other measures of combat support, such as anti-armour support, air defence, treatment of prisoners of war, controlling the territory, resources approved for logistics, establishing communications before the operation, the method of reporting to division commanders, et cetera. To put it briefly, the order is in fact the elaborated version of assignments necessary to perform this mission. Generally speaking, when you draft a decision, you make drawings for two levels below. That means I did a drawing for brigade level and lower, and the division had to elaborate assignments for brigades and battalions. The brigade has to develop its own assignments towards companies and lower, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour. It's a matter of interpretation., which is a bit different. 41, lines 9 and 10, the witness says: "Which means I give assignments to brigades." The witness actually said "two levels below." That means divisions and brigades. And the transcript reads "brigades and lower." That's why we need to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you misunderstood me. In this order, there are no assignments of mine for the brigade. My first subordinate unit is a division, and other independent units, such as the corps artillery group, such as the Battalion of Military Police, they are independent units in direct communication with me. It is the commander of the division who issues assignments for brigades and independent units. Brigade commanders give assignments to battalions and independent units. Battalion commanders give assignments to companies. Company commanders issue assignments to platoons. Platoon commanders give assignments to sections, et cetera. When you draw a decision on the map, as you can see from my decisions, I draw the areas of responsibility and the mission of the division, and those who are directly subordinate -- subordinate to me. I can only indicate brigades in that area, because I know approximately which brigades are involved, but I can only indicate the map as such, the limit to the area, and then the division commander will issue assignments to brigades, to clarify which brigade, with what resources shall perform the assignment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, on the upper left version of this document we see something in handwriting. Do you know what that is, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the signature of the army general Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Well, that's my commander and I know his signature. I hope it's not forged. I believe it isn't, because it's my own order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, how this document came to be signed by General Rasim Delic?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: I recall that. It happened, I reckon, in the last third of the month of August, in Visoko in the command post or in the building where the commander of the main logistics centre of the BH army was based. That is where the commander, Army General Rasim Delic, signed this order as well as the decision of the commander of the 2nd Corps for the execution of this operation. I believe it was done hastily. I don't know why the commander was there. He looked at the map superficially, having confidence in me that I knew what I was doing, and he just signed the order. I don't know the exact date, but I believe it was in the last decade of August. That's between the 20th and the 30th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On this day, sir, when you were in Visoko, was anyone else present? Any other ARBiH officers present?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the same day, the order was signed by General Sakib Mahmuljin for his part of the operation which was called Farz.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say the order was signed, who signed the order for operation Farz on that day?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: This order that I see in front of me was signed by the commander, Army General Rasim Delic. There is another document, the decision, which is not here, but these two go together. One cannot exist without the other. In principle, first you draw the map, and then you write this order in which assignments are elaborated. Both were signed that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you say "the map," can you tell the Trial Chamber what you're referring to when you say "the map."

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: The geographic map on the scale of 1 to 50.000 or 1 to 100.000 -- no, it was 1 to 25.000. That is a form of decision wherein assignments are drawn, the assignments stipulated by this order. In course of preparations -- you saw the previous document presented by the Prosecution. It indicates some of my activities in developing these two documents. After those preparations, the schematic of the decision was drawn after which this entire order was written as a textual form of stipulating the assignments. Under me, there were divisions and independent units, the corps artillery group, the MP battalion and some other units who were within my force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, we see on the upper right hand portion of this document it indicates that this is copy number 2 of your order. Does that have any significance?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: It does. It does. It was my practice, at least, to save all those documents, and the first copy was the one that was used and that was filed. For purposes of the secrecy of the forthcoming assignment, it has to be known how many copies were made and where each copy is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could we please -- if the registry could assist. Could we please go to the last page this document. I know that it's page 9 in English. While that's -- while the English version is coming up, sir, do you see the Bosnian -- the original of the Bosnian language version of this document?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you explain why there does not appear to be a signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: You're right. There's no signature. I can't recall precisely why the signature is missing. It's probably the second copy. I must have brought two copies of that order and the first one was signed only, because it was done hastily, as I said, and the commander probably signed both, although the second one did not bear my signature. But this is certainly the -- the order and that is my plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender this document PT010918 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just ask one or two questions about this document before we do so. General, I would like you to just clarify something for me. I still don't understand why this document had to be signed by General Delic there, the commander of the army. And -- and the reason I'm asking this question and -- is because at page -- page 39, line 4 you say: "By planning, you see, nobody was supposed to approve it." Your plans were not being approved. You -- because these were operational plans that you did on the field, as I understood you. And I'd -- I want to find out: Is this one of such plans? And if it is one of such plans, why did this one specifically have to be signed by General Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you're perfectly right, but there is an explanation. Following a normal procedure, it would be normal for everything that is carried out by the corps be approved by this superior officer; however, the reason I went to Visoko and insisted on this document, although I had received the directive, I had received prior instructions what I was supposed to do, the reason was twofold: One is that the combat operations were performed by two corps. The most narrow part of the Vozuca pocket between 2 Corps was only 5 kilometres long. There was great danger of so-called friendly fire. We knew on the basis of prior experience, because the Vozuca pocket was an area we tried to liberate unsuccessfully several times before, we knew that we needed maximum logistical support, and that's why I wanted my commander to sign it. And another purpose was to obtain some additional logistics from them. That was different because logistical support was in short supply. But if we didn't get additional resources, our losses would have been three or four times higher. If the situation had been different, I would have been able to execute all this in my area on the basis of the directive, but since we were supposed to work together with the neighbouring unit and since we had the difficulties that I explained, I thought that my commander should see and sign this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the explanation. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 402.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, General Delic, several moments ago you -- you mentioned coordination with the 3rd Corps and their Operation Farz. Can you briefly tell the Trial Chamber -- can you briefly tell the Trial Chamber how this cooperation in -- in the planning stages was undertaken, prior to the actual operation, but the planning. Can you tell us how that was coordinated between 2 Corps and 3 Corps?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the document that you have seen, three documents before this one, you saw my plan that I was supposed to execute in order to prepare for the Uragan operation. In order to do that, I also took measures of coordination with command and units of the 3rd Corps that were involved in the operation. By that I mean that I organised coordinated action so that we could coordinate the assignments of units in territory and in time to avoid undesired consequences for me and for the other corps. As part of that, I went with division and brigade commanders to the area of the 3rd Corps, to their forward line from which they started the attack, and familiarised officers with assignments and axes of movement, because there was very little room between us in some areas. Sometimes as little as 5 kilometres. We sometimes brought section commanders. In doing this reconnaissance on both sides, we also stipulated points of contact, so that the 3rd Corps was not supposed to cross the Krivaja River and a brook next to Vozuca, and we also specified how far my forces were allowed to go and how far the forces of the 3rd Corps were allowed to go. We also specified which targets we should fire on to realise this assignment. We established communications and we sized up the situation on both sides of the front line. We specified the features that both components should attain and how to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness now be shown the document P02496. P02496.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: While we are waiting for this document, could the witness indicate a time when he met with the leaders of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, before we talk about this document, Judge Harhoff asked if you can indicate the time or a time period when you met with the leaders of the 3rd Corps in coordinating these two operations.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, all of this was done in the course of planning and development of these documents and after the drafting of these documents. Some activities took place before; other activities after this order and the map were issued. It was not just in that case alone. Several days later the commanders of smaller ten-men units were taken to the other side and vice versa to reconnoiter. They needed to see for themselves. It was done both before and after the planning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, General Delic, approximately when this coordination activity took place and over what period of time.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: You already have on the screen one of my orders in which I designate a team made up of the most responsible and most experienced officers in my command, such as Brigadier Sulejman Budakovic, the chief of training, Osman Puskar; team leader of the intelligence, Esad Hadzic; chief of artillery, Sead Arnautovic; one of the members of the operation centre, Ferid Omerovic; and another one, I believe he was a signalsman, Mirsad Zildzic. And these men, upon my orders, went on the 2nd of September to the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, and their assignment was to resolve and adjust all that remained unclear about the execution of combat operations. It was specified when they would go and when they would come back, using which vehicles, as well as who was responsible for performing this assignment, and that was my deputy, Sulejman Budakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 403.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
