utterances.text: General Delic, let me return, though, to this issue of these efforts of coordination. Can you tell us, sir, was there more than one meeting or were there -- was there one meeting where there was coordinated or more than one meeting?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I personally attended a number of those meetings. I don't know exactly how many division commanders there were. As far as I remember, on the side of the other corps there was the 35th Division; on my side, there were three divisions. What they did according to their own plan, I don't know, but I organised it myself personally three times. Maybe they organised more of such meetings. It was maybe part of their own plans and their own responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, when you -- you've made reference to the 35th Division. Do you know which units of the 35th Division were involved in Operation Farz?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: No. I can only guess. What I saw in Vozuca was that there was probably the 7th Muslim Division, the El Mujahid Detachment. I saw men with beards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness's answer was: "I can only guess." This is an objection. I would submit that for the witness to continue, it's -- he's speculating and obviously this is a key issue. So unless the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you just read the next sentence. "What I saw."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Certainly he can tell us what he saw, Your Honour, but at -- I object to him speculating about what those units may be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If he can establish a basis, of course, there's no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. But he's telling us only what he says he saw. He says, I can guess about the units involved, but then what I saw is this in Vozuca. So he's talking about what he saw only.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. If he's telling us what he -- what he saw, I have no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, I'm going to move on now to the actual --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was that question answered fully, on what he saw?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, it was, Your Honour. We'll return to that subject, actually, when the witness was in Vozuca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Hopefully before the next break or before my time expires, whichever comes first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, let me ask you now, sir, did there come a time when Operation Uragan was put in place?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Operation Uragan had its beginning and its end. The beginning was on the 10th of September, 1995 at 0600 hours. Its conclusion was on the 12th of October, 1995, upon receiving notification that combat activities should cease. It was in the evening on the 11th. Perhaps around 23 or 24 hundred hours. That's when that directive came in and for me, as commander, practically that was the end of the operation. It lasted some 30-plus days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, General Delic, I want to focus your attention on day one; that is, 10 September 1995. Can you tell us what -- again, briefly, sir, because of time limitations, can you tell us what happened on that day beginning at 0600, when the attack was launched.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was at the front end of defence of the besieging forces, and I had a visual command of all that was happening in the theatre, covering almost 80 per cent of the area that was attacked. My units broke through the enemy lines at 6.30 along the main axis, and they immediately completed their immediate, initial task. Along the auxiliary axis, due to great losses, the 25th Division managed to complete it as late as that noon. It was then that they broke through the line and completed their immediate task. Vozuca itself and the inner portion of the pocket was taken somewhere until the evening hours on the 10th of September. Therefore, in the evening the planned immediate and following tasks were completed. It was planned for the operation to take more days; however, we managed to complete it during that day, since enemy lines were disorganised and they withdrew in depth. Therefore, on the very first day, we completed the immediate and following task approximately as planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness be shown PT02560. That's P02560.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, do you see the document on the screen in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This document comes from my command under my approval. My deputy drafted it, Sulejman Budakovic. This is his signature. This document was drafted at the forward command post of the 2nd Corps in the village of Cubric, Banovici municipality. It was forwarded to the operational centre of the General Staff in Kakanj, personally to the chief of staff. It was forwarded to the forward command post of the 3rd Corps, also to the commander personally. Perhaps if you want me, I can comment on its contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: It states what was done during the 10th of September. This document was created before 10.00 or slightly later, but it says up until 10.00 the 2nd Corps seized facilities at elevation 282, elevation 433, Borik, to the south from the village of Mrahonivici [phoen], Hrustovica Brdo [phoen], trig point 397, trig point 452, the village of Kelempici, the village of Delici, and they are still working on providing security for the flanks. The units are working according to plan and progressing towards the 3rd Corps units to join them in the village of Gornje Bare. In Vozuca, a firing position of the mortar the group of 100-millimetre calibre was neutralised. Casualties up until that point: Killed 5 and 35 wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We would ask that this document be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 404.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness now be shown P02576, P02576.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you see this document, General Delic?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That is an information document sent from the morale directorate of the General Staff to all subordinate units and components of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, among others to all corps commands. It has to do on the information about the successes of units of the 2nd and 3rd Corps and the 28th ground forces division of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the Vozuca-Mount Ozren battlefield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask you -- I'd ask you, sir, to take a look at the first paragraph of this document. Read that to yourself, and I'll ask you a couple of questions about it.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you -- can you comment upon the contents of this paragraph, in terms of the accuracy or inaccuracy of the information in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: I wanted to say that to me it seems illogical that I am being forwarded information on my activities. Why would I need that? However, it seems to have been sent to me, stating the data on the things carried out and also data on how far individual units went and what they managed to seize. I believe the information contained therein is approximately correct. I don't know. I would have to consult my maps and reports to see whether the lines are as stipulated here. In any case, those who sent it seems to have known it better than I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We'd ask that this document be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 405.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask -- excuse me. I would ask that the witness now be shown P02612. P02612.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, do you see this document on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know what this document is, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I can read it out loud, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's -- sorry, General, but we -- let me just ask you, first of all, if you can tell us what this document is.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: The Kakanj command post is reporting or forwarding to the commander, Army General Rasim Delic, some information on the latest results achieved by the Army of the Republic of B and H.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, do you see the paragraph that begins "on the Vozuca-Ozren front"?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It's on page 2 in the English version. Sir, I would ask you if you could read that paragraph to yourself, and I'll ask you to comment upon it once you've had the opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: I've read the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you comment, sir, on the information contained in that paragraph of this document with respect to its accuracy or inaccuracy?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, this does not reflect accurately the situation in the field; namely, the units of the 2nd Corps alone liberated some 250 square kilometres. We also have a number of villages mentioned and stating that the 2nd Corps liberated 110 and the 3rd Corps liberated 140 square kilometres. I don't know where that came from, but I believe as to the villages mentioned, they indeed were liberated in the first two days. I presume this information was obtained through someone from the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that -- that we understand what you're saying, sir, about what you believe is inaccurate. It's -- it's your evidence that your corps, the 2nd Corps, liberated more square kilometres than are indicated in this document?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I think this figure is a poor assessment or they were told this by anyone. I know these features mentioned here, and I think the area was larger. Another thing is that I'm not completely convinced that all of the features that had to be mentioned are indeed here. I'm trying to recall the first two days, and the line reached by that stage seems to be approximately as mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders P02612 into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Document P02612 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 406.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask that the witness now be shown P02793. P02793. Actually, if we could see the entire document, please. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, do you see this document on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This document, sir, appears to be dated December 1999. Can you -- can you explain to the Trial Chamber what this document was or is?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. In 1999 or perhaps towards end 1998, at the level of the then-Army of the Federation, at the level of the General Staff, some 15 to 20 people with Ph.D.s were tasked with the task of producing this. As for any commanders -- commands which were still in existence and those that had been disbanded by that time and also those that were transferred to the Army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, were tasked with procuring information needed to put together a joint analysis of the last few years of the war. They needed to describe all combat operations undertaken during the war with the lessons learned and experience derived from that. I don't think it said anywhere, but one of the goals was, I believe, that a scientific plane, there was a need to record everything that took place during the war. It was for the future soldiers to use with all lessons learned. This tactical analysis is the result of that activity. This was a task for the corps. It was for the first time that the corps did something on a tactical level. It engaged all of its units and this analysis was done in December 1998. It was pursuant to an order that was in place that required that an analysis be conducted concerning all combat operations. Not only Vozuca but others in which we gained or lost territory, and what was analysed were the temporal factors, the units that participated, et cetera. I don't think it bore the fruit it was expected to, since several years elapsed; in the meantime, some officers were not there any longer; some had died by that time. So I don't think the project was very successful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yes, you can proceed now. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, page 57, it seems to be disappearing from the screen, but the witness was talking about the activities of the corps conducted independently. I no longer see that part on -- of the transcript, but I think instead of "independent," only "activities" are being mentioned. I have serious objections to interpretation today, and I will request that tape be provided of General Delic's testimony for my review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not able to solve the problem by just saying to us what should have been said instead of "independent"?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps the question can be put by the Prosecutor. He mentioned the first independent activity of the corps in the field, and that was not recorded. I cannot locate that part. I might be able to do so during the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I can make it easier. It was the only operation conducted by the corps independently during the war. Until then, they're not in the position to engage 10.000 people in order to implement an operation. That is why the corps command was tasked with it. There was an order, I believe, in existence. I headed a team, together with my deputy commander and the commander of the 25th Division. There was another group of people, and the task was as I described. We had to try to record the truth with the lessons learned for generations to come. However, I don't think the very goal of the tactical analysis was clearly described to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first sentence in the witness's interpretation -- the witness's answer is the way it should have been recorded initially. I will try to verify that against the recording during the break. Your Honour, even what I'm saying is misinterpreted and it seems to be going on the whole day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I want to confess I'm not -- I'm at a loss. I'm not quite sure what we're talking about now. I've tried to look for this -- the word "independent." I can't find it. You keep standing up, Madam Vidovic. I don't know what you're talking about. I'm not able -- it was -- you said the first sentence was correct. "It was the only operation conducted by the corps independently during the war." Now, I get confused, because this document is dated 1999. Now, if -- if this document was the only independent activity conducted by the corps during the war, my question is: Did the -- was the war still going on in 1999? So I thought this was a study after the war for lessons that could be learnt from the previous experience. Or am I -- am I demonstrating how lost I am?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you are completely correct. The war had ended and an order came from the General Staff of the Army of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Let me stop you there. [Microphone not activated] Let me stop you there. Because it's when we talk too much that we get confused.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If the war had stopped, this was just a study, as you told us at the beginning when you dealt with this document, that it was done by a number of Ph.D.s to learn the lessons of the war. Okay. So it was not -- is it therefore correct or incorrect to say, as -- as it is stated here at page 59, line 3: "It was the only operation conducted by the corps independently during the war"? Is that statement correct or is that a misstatement or a misinterpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the only and the last one, the first and the last operation conducted independently by the corps during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An operation is the most extensive type of activity in which the entirety of a corps -- combat activity in which an entire corps is included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me understand. What is this operation that was conducted independently during the war by the corps? What is this operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the only operation such as that was the one under the code name Uragan 95. There were no others, since most of the units of the corps could not be engaged in a single task. Before that, we had no manoeuvring units and the conditions were not in place to engage most of the corps, because the corps would have to command, organise, and implement that. It was the only operation under the command of the corps. Before that, operational groups, divisions, and brigades and battalions and smaller groups carried out such tasks. Those were combat activities and battles, the two types of activities conducted by brigades. Operations are conducted by larger units. The largest unit at the time was the corps. It engaged all of its forces within its area of responsibility that were subordinated to it to carry out a large task. This was the first and last time that we conducted an operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, sir. Okay. Obviously I was lost. It looks like you're talking about Operation Uragan and not talking about this document, the -- the drafting of this document. Is that -- do I now understand the situation better? And maybe then if you can raise your objection, Madam Vidovic, I will understand it better.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my objection was only to interpretation. I managed to locate the thing that was wrong. I try hard to follow what the witness is saying and the transcript, and he said precisely what he just repeated; namely that, the corps for the first time performed these activities independently. What was on the record - and I draw your attention now, lest you think that I'm wasting the Court's time, on page 57, lines 24 and 25 - instead of what the witness is recorded to have said, that the corps did something for the first time independently, he said the corps did something for the first time on the tactical level. And you will notice the difference. At least that's what he said. I am not going into the interpretation of what he said. I'm just following the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. Are your concerns now settled?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would ask that the witness be shown page 5 in the Bosnian version and page 8 in the -- or which is page 8 in the English version of this document. I'm sorry, I need -- I'm sorry, I need the next page in the Bosnian version. And the top -- the top half of -- the top half of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, I would ask you if you could focus your attention on the first full paragraph on this page, if you could read that to yourself and familiarise yourself with the contents, I'll ask you some questions in a moment.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you comment, sir, on the information contained in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether this is an information or a brief. It's part of that analysis, as far as I understand, and it describes what happened on the 10th September, from the beginning of the attack, until the end. It's an analysis of that activity. I don't think it's a brief. It's part of the analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Does it -- does it describe accurately what happened on that day, or is there information in this paragraph that's inaccurate, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: It's certainly accurate, because I was at the head of that team.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: And my deputy was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 25th Division was also on that team. We took all their documentation from the archives in the corps room. We had those plans presented publicly. So these details are 99 per cent accurate, I believe, in terms of territories and time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders P02793 into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Pardon. P02793 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 407.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness again be shown an electronic version of Exhibit 380. And if we could focus on the bottom half of the map, perhaps. That's fine. That's fine. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, General Delic, can -- based on these documents that we've just reviewed and your knowledge of what happened on the 10th of September, 1995, are you able on this map to indicate which part of the Vozuca pocket was liberated on that day?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: This map is now rather blurred, and I don't see the lines. I had that electronic pointer somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I think -- I think, actually, we probably need to move the map a little bit up.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: On the 10th and the 11th, somewhere east to this mark "3rd Corps," that's where the line was -- rather, west of the 2nd Corps marking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Could you please take the pen, and can you circle that part of the Vozuca pocket that was liberated on day one, that is, 10 September 1995, if you're able to do so.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Maybe I could more closely circle the 11th, but I'll try. I think this is the line. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, General Delic, we need to be very clear about what you've marked. What is to the south of that red line that you've just put on this map?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: South of that line is the place called the Vozuca with the dominant features overlooking the place itself. In the previous report you showed, the villages and hamlets that were liberated are clearly indicated. I remember only one of them, because it has the name Delic, like me. So we occupied those dominating features, and we continued activities from there on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I just want to be sure everyone understands what you're saying, sir. I -- was the Vozuca pocket or was part of the Vozuca pocket liberated on the 10th of September, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Namely, the part that was of key importance to the Banovici-Zavidovici road, including Vozuca and some villages and hamlets north of Vozuca: Sljivici, Donjici, et cetera, as well as some other dominant features I remember, Klupe, and some other features.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Are you able, sir, on this map to circle the area that was liberated by the 2nd and 3rd Corps on 10 September 1995?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: I'll try. [Marks]. Roughly that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We'd ask that this map be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This map is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 408.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would that be a convenient time, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I've been informed by the Registry that I'm at the time which I'd estimated the direct would take. I would ask, with the Court's indulgence, that I be permitted to complete the direct examination, which I expect will take some 35 to 45 additional minutes that. That includes a 15-minute video clip. I will instruct the witness to try to make the answers a bit more concise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, I know we're all endeavouring to get you home as soon as possible and the best way to guarantee that that happens is to please focus on the question and answer just the question that's asked of you. I -- as I indicated earlier, you have a broad knowledge of these issues, but if you could please try to constrain your answer to the question I asked, I would be very grateful to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point in time, we would ask that the witness be shown a video or a clip from a video which is from P06085. And, sir, I'd ask that you please look at the screen in front of you and watch this videotape. There is a transcript of this video for benefit of the court -- of the interpreters, but the first two or two and a half minutes, the transcript is yet to be produced, so I would ask if the in-court interpreters could deal with the first two to two and a half minutes and then the remaining part of the tape a transcript has been produced.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Attention. At ease. Dear soldiers, I congratulate you on this victory once again. Once again, I thank you on behalf of all our people for what you have done. I came to see you. What you have done is very important, this victory on Vozuca is an important episode in our struggle. Why? On one hand, it linked up two corps of our army that have been separated for a long time. On the other hand, it linked up Zenica and Tuzla, two of our great future centres on which our country relies. You have accomplished a great mission, therefore. Rahmet [phoen] to those who fell in this fight. And thank you, you remain the pride and the hope of these people. We managed to occupy most of the Vozuca pocket, around 106 kilometres in one day. We are continuing towards Upper Bosnia, and we wish to link up further and to -- to continue towards Maglaj. Here is Krivaja and here are we. We reached -- and which road did we take? We took this road, you see, the beautiful valley of Krivaja, Kljuc is there. Paljenik. We passed this way. And here is the completed section. The village of Stog, Stosnica, and Vozuca is here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The transcript continues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps the booth could assist us. We have provided the transcript. I -- I understand it's not synchronised to this tape, but we have provided the transcript of what's being said to the language booths, but I'm apparently not getting any interpretation, at least in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We understood that we had to do the first two minutes of -- that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry, that -- perhaps I -- I misspoke. What we indicated was that there was no transcript for the first two and a half minutes, but with the transcript we would ask that that be read in conjunction with what's being said. I apologise for the misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If you could rewind, then.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Hurricane -- we managed to capture most of the Vozuca pocket, around 150 square kilometres in one day. After the present day, we seized -- and now we continue along this ridge from Karacici towards Bocinja Gornja and, if God wills, we want to get connected with Maglaj and have our road so that we can use it and you can use it without hindrance. IZETBEGOVIC: That is Bosna? Yes, this is Bosna. And where is the Krivaja here? The Krivaja is here, in the middle, and here are we. We're here? Yes. Yes. We are here. Where did we come from now? We have come from Zavidovici. Which road did we take? We took this road, you see. The Krivaja Valley is here, Kljuc. The shouting in the background, Tekbir, Allahu Akbar. Paljenik, we passed this way, and here is the collapsed section, the part that has collapsed, the village of Stog, Stosnica and Vozuca is here. MAHMULJIN: Now tell the president approximately where the village is, to the left and right stretch, where one could settle. HASANAGIC: The villages stretch on the right and on the left-hand side of the Krivaja River. On the right of the Krivaja River, those are the villages that were earlier inhabited by the Muslim people. The entire region is Gareb and has several hamlets, but mainly that area. On the left are Adzici and Hadzici. Hadzici is now Miljevici Kalajisi, and again this part with Vozuca. There are 28 villages. How many have been liberated now? All of them. All of them have been liberated now. Has anybody counted how many houses there are that can be inhabited? How certain is it that Chetniks cannot come back again? We settle people here again and then they will be -- Our troops are now more than 13 kilometres north of here. Sejo! President, here is the exact answer. Chetniks cannot come here ever again. The problem is the struggle with those who have been left behind, that is. Some pockets here and there. No, those are two, three, or four who go together. That's the only problem. Today we are cleansing those two and, if God -- God willing, I think we'll finish that today. And as far as they're concerned, I don't know, it will take 10 days? 10, 15 days at the most. Can Chetniks in the future retake it in a counter attack? That would be a tragedy. No way, they cannot. I'm interested -- you know what I'm interested in? If we settle people here and then tomorrow they get killed again. You understand? You come up to Vijenac and you will see which facilities are up here, how strong they are, and then you will see for yourself whether that ... We intend to settle the people from Srebrenica here. They have experienced trouble once. It should be like a bottleneck. Only through that bottleneck can it ... That's what I'm asking. With this we release two brigades, more than two brigades. Now we can -- 4.000 people. 4.000 people who can go guard it. Even more with me. And will it be necessary to do it -- the roofs to be done well and -- The combat continues and the combat is in progress at this point in time. We have not -- HASANAGIC: The combat is in progress at present too. The advance is made towards Karcic along this part towards -- the yesterday alone the 2nd Corps liberated 18 kilometres. As far as I understood you, Mr. President, you want to guarantee the Chetnik cannot come back here any more. Here are two corps commanders with our commanding officers, who can guarantee you the Chetnik will not appear here any more. That's the gist. IZETBEGOVIC: I agree that people come to settle, before, I am quite sure it will not again happen to them to be -- because they've had enough of that. CENGIC: There is yet another certainty, President. Now we have more new artillery and we can fight their artillery back. IZETBEGOVIC: Fine. That's -- Therefore, Mr. President, we initially intended -- our plan was to take Klupe, Kablovac, Plajenik and to make here, this is -- to make a cut here in the initial plan. The second more optimistic option was this here above Seona and so on. What we said would be most ideal. The most ideal was Plavetno Brdo, Kvrge and Podsjelovo. However, Chetniks are in a panic and we are going on further. Here you see this and this. This is in the course of the day. We are going further. I wouldn't explain further intentions now. It is not important anyway. Here are those who are taking footage, but for your information the combat actions are still in progress. Advances are being made. We shall make an effort to secure the lines that have been reached. We shall advance as much as there is a chance for it. IZETBEGOVIC: What has the 2nd Corps done regarding this coloured section and what -- This has been done by both. IZETBEGOVIC: I mean territory-wise. To be honest, this was all a joint action. I think it is a coordinated action, and we will not have -- we do not remember having a better coordination. There was not a specific demarcation either as to who is to participate where. IZETBEGOVIC: And the units which took part? The 1st Manoeuvre Battalion from Zenica, 375th Liberation Brigade from Tesanj, 7th Muslim Brigade, Special Sabotage Detachment, complete 329th Brigade, which was here, 3rd Manoeuvre Battalion, the El Mujahid Detachment with the 3rd, the 5th, 2nd Manoeuvre Battalion, 328th Brigade, and 4th Manoeuvre Battalion from Zavidovici. That was that and all those others. I beg your pardon? HASANAGIC: And the 28th Brigade. MAHMULJIN: 328th? I said that. So those were the units together with all those support units that took part on behalf of the 3rd Corps. I mean, taking also into consideration the garrison manpower and all those, there were between 12 and 14 thousand men on this side. Everything you needed. Here we had a significant support. For the first time we had around 1.000 members of the work obligation units, meaning the men who carried the wounded, fortified the lines and so on, where we met a lot of understanding. And Sejo can tell you who took part on behalf of the 2nd Corps. SEAD DELIC: Mr. President, we took part deploying three complete divisions, all manoeuvre units, which means the 21st, 22, and 25th. And all those divisions set aside their manoeuvre divisions except the 24th and the 28th. All in all, some 5.200 attackers plus a brigade and 250 each. 225th and 224th, which took part as the garrison units, which were deployed at this side at front, practically all the way to here, to these lines. That was the demarcation line. I estimate some thousand. And where was the connecting point connecting? Well, I'll show you now on the ground. If you see up here this is the highest elevation, it's called Pavlaka, a battalion of mine from there got connected. HASANAGIC: Here. It's here. DELIC: With the forces in the 3rd Corps and the attack was launched from above by the coordinated forces. We, however, for the purposes of coordination and other issues drew the line. Krivaja was mine. It was mine completely. DELIC: And the Krivaja, the road and the Krivaja were approximately -- the facility Prokop was the line. Here it is. Prokop and the valley of this river -- HASANAGIC: Kamenica. DELIC: The Kamenica, the valley of the Kamenica River. Therefore, from here, this is beside the units from the 2nd Corps were carrying out the attack. You have heard that the attack began at -- the operations lasted intensively until 3.00. A breaking point occurred by 3.00 and then the Chetniks were already in disarray and the rest was practically only a pursuit. Up here if you can -- I can bring you up to the observation post. This is, I think, the biggest war booty we've had so far and the biggest loss we have inflicted on them by now. I estimate that there are over 200 killed in my zone. Therefore, my figure is correct. There are over 200 -- [unintelligible] -- segement. And we have some prisoners, less than that though, but the equipment is enormous. So far let's say, for your information there are 7 armoured -- there is one tank T-72, one T-55, two self-propelled batteries, one 90, and one 57/2, one Praga, there is one Bofors, there are three Howitzers, one 22, some 30 to 40 different vehicles, trucks, accompanying ammunition and the rest. MAHMULJIN: Don't say in Hadzija's presence. Not in Hadzija's presence. Not all, he has not listed everything. DELIC: I estimate that several hundred thousand pieces of small ammunition were found too, but -- here I would say that even in the time of peace I never experienced that everything was running according to plans. It's a proof that we established a very good coordination with the 3rd Corps. We were even sending the company commanders to go on both sides in order to know what kind of terrain was on both this and the other side. To my knowledge, not a single bullet was fired by a 2nd Corps soldier against the 3rd Corps soldier. The lines were marked extremely well and at every moment we knew who was supposed to do what. The artillery's support of both corps was extremely good. I would particularly thank the 3rd Corps. I had an impression that they had more ammunition. Hadzija, you take care how you will handle that. MAHMULJIN: We used it better. DELIC: Let me tell you that only in that zone I had seven -- [unintelligible]. It has never happened in the 2nd Corps that in such zone seven Howitzers and five tanks launched an attack. On this line now, for example, there are four tanks that climb to the top. IZETBEGOVIC: Found some food. DELIC: We do not want that of the infidels. The rest -- CENGIC: He doesn't want to say that in my presence. BRZINA: President, so that you wouldn't think that we are less worthy. What the 2nd Corps commander told you about seizing those tanks -- they were fleeing in front of us. We were chasing them. DELIC: Fleeing, fleeing -- and fled from him. And then I told him: There is a tank, and a self-propelled battery and a Praga. Go there. Look for them. They fled in that direction. Therefore the distribution is okay, I think. IZETBEGOVIC: While we are celebrating, somebody is standing guard up there, isn't it? We are fighting now too. We are as close as here. He tells me, President. AWAD AIMAN: We imprisoned one Chetnik who says that he served the military in Doboj. DELIC: We have some six teachers imprisoned. There are those who have stayed alive, but I don't know if they still are. They were. Generally, there were many of them who -- [unintelligible] -- for a month. They created biggest problems for us. We launched four attacks from 6.00 to 1.00. We couldn't break through in this central area. We broke out at 7.00 here on the axis between Lozna and Seona. We broke through there and we were almost close to Djurica Vis in order to get connected. However, with God's help, things developed for the better. Even in the time of peace at training I wouldn't expect better. IZETBEGOVIC: Is there a room here where a conversation with civilians could take place? Probably there is. In the police administration. MAHMULJIN: If you wish to stay here, we shall move away a bit. IZETBEGOVIC: Thank you. I would just want to see the board chairman here. UNIDENTIFIED VOICE: Civilian authorities. There is room up there. It's hot. Perhaps it's better if the President takes a break. I wouldn't want the President -- because it's humid, or do you prefer it here? IZETBEGOVIC: Then it's better here. MAHMULJIN: Here, then we shall move all the others away. DELIC: I want to congratulate the 3rd Corps soldiers on a brilliantly performed operation in cooperation and coordination with the 2nd Corps. This is a textbook example of how something should be done and I can tell all the members of the 3rd Corps that they were superheroes. This is a victory that both corps could only wish for. I hope that we shall meet in Doboj again and experience the same we experienced here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, you stood up.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. If my learned friend could check this video and compare the contents with what is on the record, because I believe the transcript doesn't really reflect what the speakers were saying. It seems that the names were confused. For instance, when Mahmuljin was speak, it says "Cengic." If my learned friend could check that and give us the transcript. I think the names of the speakers are not properly recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, I guess it will have been very difficult to -- to follow up with the speed of the -- of the -- of the video. The transcript is coming. We'll -- we'll double-check that. Yes, Madam Lattanzi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. I have a problem too. When there was talk about 200 dead, in the French version -- I also have little problem because -- in the transcript, we talked about prisoners mentioned -- and I would have liked to understand this, but unfortunately I did not. So can we please check what was said. It was when -- On page 4, line 6, 200 killed -- 200 dead and there was something about prisoners of war. This is not on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did I understand you, Mr. Mundis, to say that a transcript of this is coming?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: There is a transcript of this, Your Honours, and perhaps what we can do is, if I'm able to establish a -- a foundation with this witness and get the tape admitted perhaps in the near future, we can substitute a version of that tape that has the synchronised transcript at the bottom. We were simply unable to do that in the time constraints that were on the -- on us. But we can certainly substitute a -- a synchronised version that would match, as Your Honours have seen, with respect to some of the other videotapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mundis. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, this videotape that we just watched, do you know, sir, when that videotape was made?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. However, I was wrong. Although this footage was shown to me in Sarajevo, before I was convinced that it was on the 10th of September. However, I can see in the discussion here that it was on the 11th of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, General Delic, where was this videotape made?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: This videotape was made in the place called Vozuca by the road next to the school in that settlement. I was late to that meeting. I arrived late, as can be seen from the footage. I remember that event. I didn't know that the late President Alija Izetbegovic would come. He came unannounced to see what the situation was in the theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately what time this video was made on the 11th of September, 1995 in Vozuca?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: I think it was during the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders this video clip into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The video clip is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 409.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mundis, I don't know. You may perhaps still have questions for this witness arising from this video. From myself, there are a number of things I would like to establish while this witness is available from this video. But I see your opposite member is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Sorry, I was a little late standing up there, but we -- we're happy for the video to be admitted into evidence subject to the caveat that an accurate transcript be provided to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Certainly, certainly, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely. And we'll notify the Chamber and the Defence when the synchronised version is available, and if there are concerns concerning the accuracy of the translations, I'm sure the Defence will notify us, and we'll take whatever steps are required to make sure that the transcript and translation thereof are -- are accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, now, this video clip that you've just watched, can you identify any of the people that were visible on that videotape?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know it by heart. I still remember it, and this was a good reminder, this footage. The late President of the Presidency, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic; Minister of the Interior, Mr. Bakir Alispahic; Minister of the Interior of the County or the then -- or the current canton of Tuzla, Mr. Rancic, the president of the then canton Izet Adzic [phoen], commander of the logistics centre of the GLLC, the main logistics centre of the Army of the Republic of BiH, Hadzija Cengic [phoen]; commander of the 7th Muslim Unit, General Halid Brzina; commander of the 3rd Corps, Sakib Mahmuljin; commander of the 35th Division of the 3rd Corps, I think his last name was Hasanovic. I'm trying to recall the rest. There were another two people. I believe they were from the municipalities of Maglaj and Zavidovici. I don't know them; however, I presume these were the people. There were some other people in the President's entourage, but I forgot what their names were. In this footage, you can also see the chief of staff of the 25th Division, from my division, Mr. Enver Delibegovic. Also in the footage, as far as I could see, there were members of the 7th Muslim Brigade. I don't know them by -- or I don't know them individually, but I could see some soldiers or perhaps officers of the El Mujahid Detachment. I don't know their names, though, and I am unable to identify them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am aware of time constraints. I do have five still photographs. I think it would be helpful if the witness could perhaps mark them and indicate on the identity of some of the individuals contained on the videotape. I do believe that would be assistance. So perhaps with the assistance of the usher, these five photographs could be put on the ELMO, and the witness can perhaps identify people on the tape. And I do have also a set of these for the Defence, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's start with -- start with that photo. Just if you could leave them all there, please. Now, General Delic, on the -- on the -- General Delic, on the -- on the machine to your right where the actual photo is -- we can't mark this one. Sir, don't mark this one on the computer, but on the actual picture next to you. The gentleman in the -- do you know the gentleman in the green short-sleeved T-shirt?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the chief of staff of the 25th Division. He was also my chief of staff while I commanded the 5th operational group, commander of the municipal staff, Adilja Delibegovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, could you please take the pen marker that the usher is handing you and just write his name, perhaps on his green T-shirt, so that we know exactly it is you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, the individual wearing the suit, the civilian suit, do you know what who that is, and can you put his name on there, please.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: If I may, this is the late President of the Presidency, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And do you recognise the person who's wearing the military cap?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Commander of the 3rd Corps, General Sakib Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps, we would ask that -- I don't know if it's easier to tender all of five of these as one exhibit, perhaps. If we could then go to the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise any of the individuals in this photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. This is the commander of the 35th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanagic. I think his rank was there of a brigadier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, General Delic. And anyone else in this photo that you recognise?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: I have already identified these two men. I don't know who the rest are. This is General Sakib Mahmuljin and the late President, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps, again, sir, if you could just please write their names on -- on ...

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you could then take the next photograph, please, that's in front of you, and put that on -- on top of -- take the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Were there more names that he recognised on that last photo?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise anyone else, sir, on that previous photograph, with Mr. Hasanagic, Mr. Mahmuljin, and President Izetbegovic? Do you recognise any of those other people?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: No. I think it is one of the officers of the 3rd Corps. I don't know his name, though, the one standing behind the late President Izetbegovic. I think he was from the engineers or communications, but I don't want to speculate. This is me, younger. This is General Brzina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, again, sir, for clarification, what position did -- what -- what -- sorry. Sorry, sorry. What position did General Brzina hold?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: General Brzina commanded the 7th Muslim Brigade. It was a motorised brigade, the 7th Muslim Brigade. This -- this is Mr. Izet Hadzic. He represents the civilian authorities. He was the president of the county. I can't make out the other faces. Perhaps we could see them better in one of the forthcoming photographs. Out of the faces here, I can recognise the commander of the Main logistics centre, Mr. Halid Cengic. [Marks]. This is us here. I can identify the people by their uniform. You can see me here again. I do not recognise any others. In this photograph, this is the late President of the Presidency, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. Then the commander of the 3rd Corps, Mr. Sakib Mahmuljin. I think these two -- well, at least one, either/or, is from the El Mujahid Detachment; however, I don't want to speculate, since I don't know their names and I never communicated with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In fact I was going to ask the -- that if there are any people whose names Mr. Delic doesn't know, but if he knows their rank -- or their positions and what unit they belonged to, he must tell us what they were. He has just done that which -- he says "either one of these two is from the El Mujahid." I'm going to have to ask you to go through the other pictures to -- to see if he can --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- identify any of the other people at --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let -- perhaps, Mr. President, I'll do that. Let me just finish up with this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, sir, I hate to be repetitive, but can you please write the names of the individuals who you recognise on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, Sakib Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you've -- you've indicated that one of those -- one of the other two gentlemen whose faces -- face is visible was from the El Mujahid. Can you circle the two people you were referring to on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Perhaps both of them. I don't know. But they were with that group there. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. And -- thank you. Now, if we could then go back to the -- to the previous picture. We're going to run quickly through the -- the four pictures again. Is there anyone else -- I don't know if you understood the Judge's -- the Presiding Judge's question. Do you recognise anyone else not by name but by position or function? If there was someone visible in this photo that you haven't marked that you know by their position or function.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Not in these photographs. I did say that I know one person. I think it was this person. He was from the 3rd Corps, I believe, from the engineers or some other branch. But I don't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, maybe -- let me just ask a very pointed question: At page 80, line 17 to 22, you said: "I don't know them by -- or I don't know them individually, but I could see some soldiers or perhaps officers of the El Mujahid Detachment." Are you able to identify an officer or a soldier of the El Mujahid Detachment on all those photographs? Okay. You have -- you have identified these two on this photograph. If you can go through the other photographs, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to tell you what I think, of course. I saw those units when I came there. I was late and they were lined up. One of them -- or a part of them had long beards, but they looked differently from the people of the 7th Muslim Brigade. I presumed they were maybe from the El Mujahid Detachment; however, I don't know any single one of them. This is not in these photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me stop you. I understand that. I'm just asking you based on the statement you made that you said you don't know them individually -- I'm not asking you to give their names. I'm just saying if you can say this is a soldier or officer of the El Mujahid Detachment in all of these pictures as you see them. I'm not asking you to -- to give their names, because you did say you don't know their names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, this is the Ramadan for us Bosniaks. I do not dare guess. I am uncertain. I immediately said that I think this is who they were. I don't know. I'm not sure what unit they belong to, since there were no one -- there was no one else who looked like that. Perhaps these two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please understand -- please understand what I'm asking you, Mr. Delic. I'm not talking about the photograph. I'm talking about the remainder of the photographs. Please can you remove the photograph and go through the other photographs and just tell us if you note anybody that you can -- that you say is an officer -- who you saw at that -- on that day as a soldier or perhaps an officer of the El Mujahid Detachment. Anybody on this picture? Anybody on that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I suspect that it could be this person, but I don't know. I didn't see him lined up or introducing himself. He looks like one of them. I saw a group of them. I don't know how many. He could be one of them, but I cannot be certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, when you said, "I don't know them by or I don't know them individually, but I could see some soldiers or perhaps officers of the El Mujahid Detachment," what did you mean? You said then -- at that page, you said you saw them. Now you're saying you are guessing, you don't know. What's the problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can explain. When I arrived, it was at the moment when the late President of the Presidency was inspecting the line-up. I was late by some five to ten minutes. The 7th Muslim Brigade were lined up, I believe. I think it was that unit. And they looked differently from the El Mujahedin. They had no beards. They were neat. And I concluded that those other people were not from the 7th Brigade but from the El Mujahid Detachment. No one else could have looked like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just explain what my question is to you about. I'm not asking you about the line-up that was done by the previous President. I'm asking you to look at these photographs, all of them, and just identify the people that you say you saw as soldiers or perhaps officers of the El Mujahid. And if you -- now, I -- that I can understand what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to maybe take the floor here. Maybe I understood something differently because I'm following the French version and not the English version. But in the beginning -- could we have the -- the photograph where there were the two people which he believes could belong. Thank you. So when we started and he saw this picture, in the French interpretation, I understood that he was just guessing that they might be. He wasn't really sure. Did I understand you right? Because that's what I got from the French translation. I don't know what's in the English transcript, but from the French this is what I understood that, the witness was just guessing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you understand -- you understood well. That is what I meant. I suppose. I don't know them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: General, do you remember which language they spoke?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My feeling was that both of them spoke to the late President, and I think they spoke Bosnian. I don't think there was anyone there interpreting, as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We would move the five photographs that the witness has marked into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The photographs are admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 410.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, on this day, 11 September 1995, do you know where General Rasim Delic was?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: I suppose I might be wrong in terms of country, but I think he was in either Indonesia or Malaysia. However, he was abroad. That is the correct answer. He wasn't in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And just so we're clear then, sir, on the 11th of September, 1995, General Rasim Delic was not in Vozuca with these other individuals that we saw on the tape.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, that the -- the next time after this meeting, that is, after 11 September 1995, do you recall the next time you saw General Rasim Delic?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: I recall the place and the event when I saw him. It was in the Lukavac municipality, the settlement of Vijenac, to the south-west from the municipality of Lukavac at one of the observation posts where I acquainted him with the situation. The time is late August. The last third of the month of August, between the 20th and the end of the month or perhaps the 18th or 19th towards the end. In the last third, the last decade of the month of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps it's an interpretation error. I'm asking you about after September 11th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: September. I apologise. Not August. September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness be shown P02656. P02656. Do you see the document on the screen in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this document relates to?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: This document was drafted by the morale administration in Sarajevo on the 24th of September, 1995. It contains information on a visit to the units which participated in the liberation or the liberation operation by the army general commander Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution would move this document into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 411.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, we heard on the earlier videotape about the issue of prisoners of war during the operation to liberate the Vozuca pocket. Can you briefly - again briefly, sir - tell us about any information you had concerning prisoners of war taken during that operation and particularly in the first day or two of that operation.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: The first day, the situation was quite unclear. The overall balance of what was recorded and what the situation was in the field was that within the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps, I think 163 people were caught. It may have been 136 instead of 163, but I think it is 163. Another 30 soldiers were taken prisoner by the Olovo Brigade in the surroundings of the town of Olovo, to the south of there by some 30 or 40 kilometres. Therefore, the total figure is around 183. The 163 captured were registered by the International Red Cross. At the beginning of 1993, they were all handed over safe and sound to the authorities of the smaller entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry, General, it may have been a -- an error or a translation error. The English transcript refers to them being handed over at the beginning of 1993. Is --

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: 1996, after the Dayton Accords. I don't know the exact date. February or March 1996. Around that time, in the first trimester of 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness now be shown P02702. P02702.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, do you see the document on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. The document is from the command of the 3rd -- sorry, part of the command of the 3rd Corps, the section of military intelligence service sent to the command of the 2nd Corps, that is, my command; also to the section of the military intelligence section, 5th October 1995, and it relates to the captured aggressors' soldiers and civilian persons on the Ozren-Vozuca battlefield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you -- do you know, General Delic, why 3rd Corps military intelligence service sent this document to the military intelligence service of 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I'm not sure. I can only say that due to that horizontal link and cooperation, there's nothing of particular interest. But this is about soldiers. I don't think it was particularly important to the 3rd -- to the 2nd Corps on any grounds whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'd ask that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 412.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can the witness now be shown P02720. P02720.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, do you see the document on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you see from this document who this document is -- what entity this document is from and to whom it's addressed?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: It's written at the top: "The International Committee of the Red Cross" probably,"Tuzla," dated 19 October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: To whom -- to whom is the letter addressed?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: It says: "Dear sir." And below, it's written that it's addressed to Brigadier Sead Delic, commander of the 2nd Corps in Tuzla, a copy to Mehmed Zilic, chief of the Security Service of the 2nd Corps, also to Enver Hodzic [phoen], deputy commander of the 2nd Corps of the BH army for legal affairs and president of the commission of the 2nd Corps for the exchange of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you please on the English version scroll to the top of the document. General Delic, do you see the stamp on the upper part of this document and if so, can you tell us what that is.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: It means that this document was received by the command of the 2nd Corps. More precisely, by the section of the military security service. It was received on the 25th October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'd ask that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question to ask. In the video, we have seen a while ago, at a given moment, you personally say that the prisoners are being made, some people have been taken alive, and you don't know if they are still alive or not. Was this something accurate? Did you indeed say that? And what did you mean to say with the expression "I do not know if they are still alive"? What did you mean by that expression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did say that. You know that in war those who are in perfect health are sometimes captured along with those who are wounded seriously or lightly. In that situation, I didn't have full reports about what the situation was and what happened with those people. There were not 5 but 163. But that was for the whole operation. On the first day, there were around 80. You heard me well and the translation is accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 413.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, I have two more documents to show you. And, again, I'd ask if you could please focus on my questions so that we can wrap up this part of your testimony as quickly as possible. In the summer of 1995, sir, can you tell us whether the 2nd Corps had any capabilities to intercept communications -- electronic communications or radio communications or telephone communications.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, throughout the war the 2nd Corps had very modest equipment, but it had a section for surveillance and eavesdropping on enemy forces. The equipment we had enabled all units to eavesdrop on each other. Those are very simple devices, IUP 3, IUP 33, PRC, IUP 12. On those device, it's very easy to find a frequency and listen in on the enemy. So my answer is "yes," to the extent that our equipment enabled us to eavesdrop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, General Delic, can you again, sir, briefly describe what was done with any information that was intercepted.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: All the information gathered through intercepts, if they were raw material -- and why do I say "raw material"? During the war, I sometimes organised myself false radio networks to deceive the enemy. This raw material would always be submitted to the competent intelligence authority, which would select and analyse the material. After their selection and analysis, in the measure necessary, the commander would be informed personally or the parties involved would be informed. That was the collation of that material. These persons had no other job but to note down anything they heard or taped during a radio communication they intercepted. They would then distribute it to the competent organs, which in their turn would analyse it in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness be shown P02282. P02282.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, do you see the document on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what this document is.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: It's a document compiled by radio surveillance. It's probably that section, the company for radio surveillance was submitting this information to the corps, depending on the area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note from the document that this witness's name doesn't appear in the document. And I just wondered if we could perhaps -- it's an objection. If we could ensure that we have a solid foundation before proceeding to ask questions from the witness about the contents of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness has described the process by which the 2nd Corps personnel who were responsible for such intercepts conducted such intercepts. I can ask him one or two more questions about information contained on the face of the document. Again, I'm not to the point of tendering the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you mean not to the point of tendering the document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the witness a few more questions about the document and then tender it into evidence and I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed. We'll hold the objection in abeyance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, can you tell the Trial Chamber who produced this document and to whom it's addressed.

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: It's addressed to the command of the 2nd Corps. I would like to explain to the Trial Chamber. When a document is addressed to the command of the 2nd Corps, it first goes to the office. The office then sends it to the operations centre, to an office where it is recorded and given a reference in the files. And the operations centre then forwards it to the competent organs for further action. Now, whenever intercepts were concerned, they would be sent to the intelligence organ that would analyse the contents. So this was sent by the group who intercepted this exchange. It says that it was on a high frequency -- in the high frequency range, and it's always indicated in whose area of responsibility it was. In this case, it was the 22nd Division of the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, General Delic, can you inform the Trial Chamber what this intercept in the 22nd Division AOR relates to?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can make it clear. The area of responsibility of the 22nd Division covered an area west of Tuzla: Lukavac, Gracanica, Doboj, Doboj Istok. So it was towards the town of Doboj and towards Ozren, towards the Bosna River. From Spreca River towards Bosna River. This is a conversation between two persons, one of them, as it says here Mujahid, and the other is a delta X delta Y [Realtime transcript read in error "delta your excellency"]. The time is -- I expect it probably on the same day, 22nd July. You see the transcript, of course, but this Mujahid is talking to one of the enemy soldiers or officers saying that they have one captive, and they are asking that another 100 men who are still defending surrender; otherwise, they would kill this captive by slitting his throat. You have it in the English version, so I'm not going to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, you -- you just indicated as reflected on lines 23 and 24 of page 96, a conversation between two persons, delta X and delta Y, I believe you said, which for some reason says "delta your excellency"? Can you tell us who these -- or what these delta X and delta Y represent?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: I can only suppose that those were our adversaries. So it's between Bosniaks and Serbs if I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you see, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just -- is this a conversation between two people or three people? I think the witness said the participants are Mujahid, delta X, and delta Y. And if you look at it, there's an M, there's an X, and there's a Y, as they speak. Here it is in the -- in the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Precisely. And that is how the contents of this exchange was described. This is raw material, the way it was taped. They didn't add anything or analyse anything. They just transmitted it as they intercepted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Confirmation as to whether there are two or three participants. Let's just -- can we be a little more focused in your answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Delic, right up at the top, under the line indicating "22nd Division," there's a reference to the 35th Srbacka Brigade. Do you know what that is, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: I think it's the Srbac Brigade. That's why I said those were enemy forces. They were performing combat activities somewhere in the area where this intercept was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you say, sir, "enemy forces." Which military force, to the best of your knowledge, was the 35th Srbacka Brigade a component?

utterances.speaker: SEAD DELIC
utterances.text: Please, Your Honours, in line 2 it reads: "In the 35th Srbac Brigade, camouflage nets should be delivered." That's what they were listening on. They found this piece of information in -- in a conversation. Somebody was asking somebody for camouflage nets. And then after that, we read: "We are supplying you with the original conversation held on high frequency in UVF range somewhere in Ozren." It was located as being Mount Ozren. There were three participants: One, Mujahid; one delta X; and a third, delta Y. So this is an original conversation.
